messages.subject_clean: using dsm to apply a detection function when some observations don't have distance estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am working on a project analyzing marine mammal densities from standardized vessel-based surveys over 30 years. I am familiar with spatial modeling, but fairly new to the distance sampling/density surface modeling world, and am hoping to get some guidance on implementing density models using the dsm package.

Our dataset contains 5594 harbor porpoise observations. Of those, 5396 contain distance estimates. I have fit a detection function with relevant covariates, and it performs well. Now, when I run the dsm function, including the segment data, observation data, and detection function, there is an error because not all observations have associated distances. Sub-setting the data to only include observations with distances would falsely imply absences where animals were actually observed, and would mean losing data primarily from the early ‘90’s. So my question is: in dsm, is there a way to implement the detection function, using the covariates in the segment data to estimate the strip width, and include all observations even when distance was not estimated for some (3.5% of the sightings, in this case)?

The dsm package seems excellent, and I really hope to be able to use it to its full potential. Any feedback or advice would be much appreciated.

Cheers,
Dawn

messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance samplers

I was hoping to just bounce a few comments I have acquired whilst analysing recreational vessel data.

I have two years of rec vessel data. The data collected can be further split into vessel categories (motorboat, jetski, and sailboat). After further inspection and data exploration (Fig 1 as example), it is clear the detectability of each vessel type varies (this makes sense as sailboats can be seen much further). As there were only a few jetski sightings in each year, I decided to combine jetski into the motorboat/engine category. I have done this separately for each year.

I started off with year 2 and managed to build a detection function that fit the data well and gave no warnings of spiked data. I then built spatial models with this detection function which was all fairly straightforward as the data was recorded more precisely than in year 1. [side note – I have been going back and forth with the idea of including weekday as a variable affecting detectability – some days I argue that the day of the week should not impact the observer's ability to detect a vessel.. then other days I argue on weekends when there are many vessels, observers may not detect vessels as far away as when days there are fewer vessels...though upon exploration this is not necessarily the case; ie. sometimes distances are further on weekends]

Year one on the other hand is demonstrating some seriously spiked data (Fig 2 as an example for engine data with no truncation.).

I have truncated at various distances, up to 30% of the data which seems like quite a lot to try and improve the detection function and get rid of the spiked data effect. As with most spiked data, the HR model drops off rapidly with distance to try and fit this data. It is the HR models that are getting the lowest AIC scores. However, I do not believe that detection rate for vessels falls off that rapidly, and so a half normal model is more appropriate. However, none of the half normal models show significant model fit at the 0.05 following CramerVon Mises tests. I have seen in previous discussions that sometimes the argument of which model to use is more biological than mathematical – the probability of detecting a vessel within 500 metres of the survey vessel should be near perfect, and so I am inclined to scrap the hazard rate models and go for half normal models.

I have also tried pooling the sightings across the two years to build a global detection function (research vessel/procedures were the same across both years), in hopes to reduce the spiked effect. I am still getting spiked data and warnings of spiked data, so I also looked at binning the distances into cutpoints. After playing around with it, I came to cutpoints of 450m (which seems like quite a lot!?). But I am also thinking that vessels within a 500m radius are usually pretty visible – it’s not like whales that are only at the surface for a couple of seconds.

I know this is a long email, but the major points I wanted to discuss were:
Is weekday a sensible factor to include within the detection function? I argue yes, then other days I talk myself out of it.
Do I have enough justification to pick a half-normal model that does not show significant model fit at the 0.05 level over a HR model with lower AIC and significant model fit but a low average Pa and warnings for spiked data.
Should binning at 450m be my last resort? OR it is sensible that I believe a boat is nearly perfectly detectable within 500m of the survey vessel.
DSM
Whilst I will investigate spatial models for each vessel category separately, i also hope to build a combined "recreational vessel model". I have come across the paper by Miller et al., 2021 (Extending density surface models to include multiple and double observer platforms). It is a new feature of DSM to include data with various truncation distances. Whilst the paper uses it for various viewing platforms, am I right in thinking I can apply it here in my situation? I can combine both my segmented datasets (sail and engine) together with an added column (ddf.obj) depicting the detection function for sail and engine. One thing I didn't find (correct me if I missed that point) is at what distances segments need to be "cut". As a rule of thumb, it is usually twice the truncated detection function to make it roughly square. With two varying truncations, would you use segments that capture the larger truncation?

 I apologise in advance if this email seems a little convoluted and long.

Many thanks,

Raph

Raph, a partial answer to your questions.  The key here is your comment that in year 2, ‘the data was recorded more precisely than in year 1’.  You don’t clarify this, but it seems clear that your data for year 1 are too poor to yield reliable estimates, whereas they are very good in year 2.  I would not ‘pollute’ your year 2 data by pooling with year 1!  The half-normal is rejected for year 1 primarily because distances estimates are biased, rather than because the model is poor.  I would guess that many detections have been recorded as on the line, perhaps because sighting angles were not measured accurately, and often recorded as zero.  You might have to resort to taking the year 2 detection functions, and assuming that they can be used with year 1 sightings.

No reason why you can’t include day of week (or weekday vs weekend) as a covariate, and see whether AIC prefers the model with this covariate.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dawn, list,

In some situations it causes no bias to drop the observations with
missing distances.  An example is where you are only interested in a
global density estimate and you can be sure that none of the
observations with missing distances were actually at 0 distance.  In
this case, dropping the observations with missing distances will cause
the estimated detection function to decline more quickly with increasing
distance, resulting in a lower estimated p.  So you have a lower n
because you discarded some observations, a lower p because you discarded
some observations, and the two balance out.

However, you are likely not in that situation, because it sounds like
you are interested in trends over time as well as over space, and there
was more missing data in the past than in the present.  All the same, if
you know the missing observations were not at zero distance, and you
have a time covariate in your detection function, it will still likely
be fine just to drop those observations.

In general though, I appreciate it's not ideal to drop observations,
even if it's only a small number.  So ideally you'd like to fit a
detection function to the observations that have distances and then
apply the dsm to all observations, under the assumption that the
observations without distances are missing at random with respect to
detectability (given the non-distance covariates).

I'm afraid there's nothing that I know of built into dsm to allow for
this.  (Please someone else correct me if you know otherwise!) However,
I do think we can trick dsm into doing what you want, as follows:

- Use ds (or ddf) to fit the detection function you want

- Manually add the detections with missing distances into the fitted
dsmodel object.  This part is quite painful as it involves messing
around deep inside the fitted object

- Pass the altered dsmodel object into dsm, together with an
observation.data data frame that contains the detections with missing
distances (with the distances set to some arbitrary value, less than the
truncation width but not NA)

I have written some demonstration code that works, but without
covariates.  I'm happy to send it to you if you contact me, and also to
work on a more realistic version with covariates for your dataset.
Medium term it would be helpful to make this code public so others can
use it - although a better long-term plan would be to incorporate this
functionality into the dsm package.  I can raise a feature enhancement
request but given current programmer resources it may be some time
before we get to it.  Anyway, let's correspond off the list, and post
back once we've agreed a solution.

With best wishes, Len Thomas

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am currently working on a large camera trap dataset from Cambodia and decided to incorporate the covariate Habitat (open and dense forest) in the detection function. I am trying to estimate the population density for one species of squirrel in Cambodia  and would therefore like to do a MCDS analysis and add Habitat (dense forest or open forest) as a covariate, as it is assumed a priori to affect the detection probability.

We fitted the detection functions with took 13 models into consideration:
the uniform key with 1, 2 and 3 cosine adjustments
the half normal key with 0, 1 and 2 cosine adjustments
the half normal key with 0, 1 and 2 cosine adjustments + Covariate Habitat
the hazard rate key with 0 and 1 simple polynomial adjustments
the hazard rate key with 0 and 1 simple polynomial adjustments + Covariate Habitat

You will find enclosed the summary of goodness of fit and AIC scores among fitted models. In the summary table, the P-values for all goodness of fit tests are either effectively zero and very low value, meaning none of the models fit the data because of overdispersion.

Using traditional AIC for model selection,  the best model overall had Habitat as covariate, and a hazard-rate key function with one adjustment terms. This had a lower AIC than any of the CDS models.  The result seems to indicate strong support for the notion that detection probability varied among habitats.

My question is regarding the next step about model selection of distance sampling models in the face of overdispersion. I used the first method of Howe, Buckland, Després-Einspenner, & Kühl (2019) which employs a two-step process. I first computed QAIC for each set of key function models and then ranked the models by their c^ values. But when doing this two-step process, step, which models do I take into consideration? Do I compare only models with covariate, so 5 models or do I compare again all 13 models (which means applying QAIC within key functions so for example for the hazard rate, we would have 4 different QAIC)? Depending on which methodology I use, I do not select the same models as the end.

If we compare only the models with the covariate added, the model chosen by this algorithm that adjusts for overdispersion is the same model (hazard-rate key function with one adjustment terms + cov Habitat) as would have been chosen by conventional model selection. However, if I do all 13 models, the model chosen is hazard rate key without adjustments and without the Habitat covariate.

Thank you for your answer,

Emeline

messages.body_plain:
Emeline

Before addressing your model selection question, some questions arise from looking at the table you provided.

My attention is drawn to the column of standard errors for P_a. This column tells me something about whether the parameter estimation algorithm had difficulty. For each of the models that had the habitat covariate plus adjustment terms, the standard error is very large, suggesting a problem with the estimation algorithm. You should examine the output for each model more closely, but I would suggest inference should not be made from those models, namely
HZ with simple
HN with cos 2,3 (note P_a estimate to be 0 for this model)
HN with cos 2
even HN cos 2,3 without the habitat covariate has an extremely large se(P_a). As I say, I wouldn't make inference from any of these models, regardless of what model selection tells me.  The ds()​ function in R won't allow both adjustment terms and covariates in the same model, so not sure how some of those models came to appear in your table.

After removing all the models that had algorithm problems, the QAIC model selection process might be more straightforward. Follow the steps shown in the duiker example analysis on our examples page

Thanks for the answers, surprising about the fact that the ds()​ function in R won't allow both adjustment terms and covariates in the same model, as it is the function I used and it worked. Here an example of the code I used and I put adjustment termns and covariate in the same model which did not cause error on R:

hr0 <- ds(CTDS_PLWS_VS_Effort, transect = "point", key ="hr", adjustment = NULL,

The two-step model selection procedure as you described it seems accurate.  The two-step QAIC process tries to account for overdispersion in your data by choosing simpler models that what would be chosen using conventional model selection procedures. Overdispersion causes the histogram of radial distances to be "bumpy".  Models with many parameters will try to fit those bumps. But the bumps are not caused by the detection process being modelled, but rather stationary individuals being recorded in multiple snapshot moments at the same location. That is not something we wish to model, but rather the decay of detectability as a function of distance from the camera. Hence the simpler model (without the covariate) is chosen by the modified selection algorithm.

I'm trying to duplicate the output you report (data.frame with 0 columns and 0 rows). Thus far, I've not been able to produce that output when performing a bootstrap on a data set with multiple strata and group size (namely the data set ClusterExercise​ that ships with the Distance package).

To help pinpoint the issue can I ask
what version of the Distance package are you using (version 1.0.7 is the current CRAN version)
does your BSDPPWS data frame contain a column for area of the strata? If area is not provided, an abundance estimate cannot be produced (only a density estimate). Because you are harvesting the abundance estimates from the bootstrap via the bootdht_Nhat_summarize​ function, if those abundances do not exist, code might return a data.frame with 0 columns and 0 rows). Recognize there is a companion summary function bootdht_Dhat_summarize​ for use when inference is based around density estimates.
In answer to your second question, if you have separate bootstrap outputs for the comparison you wish to make, I think the remedy is only slightly more complicated than merging the two vectors of replicate estimates, but not much.  From the merged data frame, compute the difference for each pair of estimates, make a histogram (an compute quantiles associated with the alpha level of interest). Finally you can compute the proportion of differences that are greater than or less than zero to produce your significance value. If that's not clear, we can follow up off line if you wish.
